Restate the following for a general-audience summary in no more than two sentences.

In some instances, data users may need to derive an estimate by multiplying a published count by a published percentage. For example, a data user might be interested in the number of 1-unit detached owner-occupied housing units in a geographic area. In 2015, the number of owner-occupied housing units in the United States was 74,506,512 with an MOE of 228,238, and the percent of 1-unit detached owner-occupied housing units was 82.4 (0.824) with an MOE of 0.1 percent (0.001). 66 So, the number of 1-unit detached owner-occupied housing units was 74,506,512 * 0.824 = 61,393,366. Thus, the 90 percent confidence interval for this estimate is [61,393,366 – 202,289] to [61,393,366 + 202,289] or 61,191,077 to 61,595,655. Using formula (2), the SE of the product is 202,289 / 1.645 = 122,972. Using formula (4), the coefficient of variation for this derived estimate is (122,972 / 61,393,366) * 100 = 0.2 percent, indicating that the derived estimate is very reliable.
response_text: Sometimes you can estimate a number the Census Bureau doesn't publish directly by multiplying two figures it does publish — for instance, multiplying the 74,506,512 owner-occupied homes in the U.S. in 2015 by the 82.4 percent that were single detached houses gives about 61.4 million such homes. Because both inputs carry some sampling error, the derived figure comes with its own margin of error (about ±202,000, or a 90 percent confidence range of roughly 61.19 to 61.60 million) — a spread small enough, at about 0.2 percent of the estimate, to call the result highly reliable.
